reasons: spec.md's Requirements bullet for dropped eval cases is unchanged this round and, read on its own (without the Design section), still states the dot-prefixed-rename addition and then immediately says 'A case is dropped when no path remains... so that one file dropped out of a multi-file case while a sibling survives is never mistaken for the whole case's drop (panel decision #2, phase b)' with no caveat that this sibling-survives-rescues-the-case rule does not apply to the dot-rename addition. The one new sentence from panel decision #1 lives only in the Design section further down and never cross-references or amends this Requirements sentence, so the spec still contains two bullets that, read independently, assert opposite outcomes for the exact scenario the panel just settled.

plugin/gate/checks.py's dropped_eval_cases docstring was not touched this round: it still cites only panel decision #2 and states unqualified that 'a partial multi-file deletion with a surviving sibling is never mistaken for the whole case's drop.' That sentence is now literally false for the dot-rename case (proven false by the very pinning test this round adds), and nothing in the docstring or an inline comment on the `dropped = set(dot_dropped) | {...}` line explains that the dot-rule is deliberately exempt from survivor filtering per panel decision #1. A future maintainer reading only the function (the most likely place to look before touching this code) has no signal that the current union-without-filtering is intentional rather than the bug the first reviewer reported, and could 'fix' it right back into the evasion hole the panel rejected.

plan.md's Proof/Order-of-work/Risks sections are not updated to mention the new pinning test or panel decision #1, even though plan.md's own Risks section already claims (from an earlier round) that the survivor-vs-drop gap 'is now closed by the design' -- the plan's bookkeeping of what proves what is left incomplete relative to the actual diff, though this is a secondary point next to the two above.
classification_reasons: The spec still carries an open ambiguity between two of its own sections on a security/correctness-relevant rule (fail-closed vs fail-open for a dot-rename with a surviving sibling), which is not a tight spec.

check_ratchets is a gate check that runs at phases (c), (d) and (e) for every change type in every project the plugin drives (intent.md's own 'Affected users and systems'): wide blast radius for any drift in its documented semantics.

The function itself (dropped_eval_cases) is exactly the kind of fail-closed security-relevant logic a test alone does not fully protect against regression if the documentation surrounding it keeps pointing future maintainers at the rejected reading.
attempted: Intent: confirmed the round's two stated edits (one Design sentence in spec.md, one pinning test in tests/test_gate.py) match what the delegation prompt and panel decision #1 called for; found no scope creep.

Spec and plan: compared spec.md's Requirements bullet (unchanged) against its new Design sentence (added this round) and found they are not reconciled -- read in isolation, Requirements still implies the opposite of what Design now states and what the code does. Checked plan.md for matching updates (Proof list, Risks) and found none added this round for the new test.

Proof: read tests/test_gate.py's new test_ratchets_eval_case_dot_rename_wins_over_a_surviving_sibling against the diff and the _ratchet_repo fixture (foo/a.yaml + foo/b.yaml as a genuine two-file case); confirmed it dot-renames only a.yaml, leaves b.yaml untouched, and asserts the whole case 'evals/cases/foo/' is reported dropped -- this correctly pins the exact scenario panel decision #1 described, distinct from the pre-existing single-file 'bar' dot-rename test. Did not treat any evidence/*.json or run-*.json record as proof for or against the diff.
Blast radius: check_ratchets runs at (c)/(d)/(e) for every project; no guardrail files (.claude/**, CLAUDE.md, REVIEW.md, sdlc.yaml) touched in this round's diff.

Policies: no security-baseline, data-conventions or coding-standards rule appears violated by this round's two edits themselves; the concern raised here is about documentation completeness, not a policy breach.

Tests: confirmed the new test would fail (not catch a regression) under the originally-proposed 'fix' (filtering dot_dropped against survivor_cases), so it is a genuine pin, not a tautology; did not find any pre-existing test weakened.
